Go ahead.
Do you remember anything about the military groups there used to be? There used to be some, I believe, that had rifles and did exhibitions. Do you ever remember seeing any of them?
They did drilling. They did drilling. Drilling? Yeah. Like the old sword drill. Well, they had these...

Parading with rifles. One was called the Larendon Rifles. That was the name of one of them. Do you remember of ever seeing any? I think they'd have parades and sometimes the bands would be out in front.
Yes. No, I don't.
You don't remember those? You don't remember when they had the brooms or anything, huh? No. What were some of the other things?
They had brooms and they had dumbbell brigades.
Yeah.
You might have been younger then.
Yeah.

The women would get their brooms, I understand. I don't know. Something else I've heard about is gold-headed canes. Does that mean anything to you? Every once in a while they would be presented to someone.
Do you know why they'd give anybody a gold-headed cane? No. They write it up in the paper. It must have been quite an honor in those days.
A gold-headed cane?
Yeah, a gold-headed.
Uh-huh.
Gold-handled, walking stick.
Yeah, uh-huh.
You never saw many of those yourself, huh?
No, sir.
You got more? Go ahead.
No, I think I'm-
Okay. Well, what about Labor Day? What kind of a parade would they have on Labor Day?
Oh, man. They didn't have bands enough to furnish the companies. Oh, bands. Set out in the country and get them country bands. Come fill out the parade.
You didn't ever go to school in New Orleans, did you?
No, ma'am.
You were pretty old then.
No, ma'am. My sister, she went to- How do you call that place we talking about this morning? Clock, eh? No. What place? Wicca. Wicca.
Was that a public school?
It's a college now. It's a high school now. High school.
Oh, I see. That was here in the city.
Mm-hmm.
Was your sister younger than you were?
Oh, yes. She long died.
I see.
Yes, ma'am. She was young and high.
I was going to ask you, what were some of the other jobs the brass bands played in older times?

Oh, everything was given, brass bands. Baseball park, batter band. I played in the Harmon Park. Played in the charity hospital. We had to go to the charity hospital every Sunday. Out there where the flag jumped. And we had to play out there. Willie Willeton was the leader then, you know. He died, you know.
You mentioned the Pickwick band. Do you remember anything about how that got started?
What is that?
The Pickwick band, didn't you mention that?

Oh, yeah. The Pickwick, sure. Well, I know. You see, them times, they didn't have regular men that hire you, me. Not, see? That's why they all had different uniforms. You take the Excelsons. They had full dress suits. Red, white, and blue, you know. Take the Arnold band. They had blue suits. The Pickwick, they had blue suits with different stripes in it. We had blue suits. A whole lot of mangalons. Every band used to hire men. That would make you say, oh, he ain't no member of that band. Look, he got a different suit. He'd come out and sit in such a band. That's the way they were.
These bands have been going on a pretty long time. They've been in New Orleans a long time.
Yes, they have. Isn't that right? Oh, they had some good bands, yeah.
Did you ever hear the Oriental band?
Who? Oriental. Oriental. I always talk of them. I never heard of them. Oriental.
What about Occidental? Was there an Occidental band?
Who?
Occidental.
No.
No way.
A white band.
No, I don't know. I don't know. But you say you had heard of the Pickwick. I believe that's an old one.
It is, yeah. The Onward is an old band, Exxelfy.
Yeah, Onward and Exxelfy.
Oh, the oldest band?
Yes. Exxelfy. Was the oldest, huh? Yes, yeah.
I wonder how old that was.
Uh-huh.
I wonder how old that was.
Oh, I don't know how old they were.

Oh, Pete, yeah, Pete.
He would know that. He had that band.
Pete was a violin player, you know. Uh-huh.

That's right. That's right. You know George Moretti.
I heard about him. I wondered if Wooden Joe ever had a brass band. You remember Wooden Joe?
Sure, he played with me. Oh, yeah? Yeah. Wooden Joe, he died downtown. Trumpet player.
Yeah.
Sure, he played with me.
What brass band was that he was having?
That was Eureka. He played in Eureka.
Did he have his own band in the street?
No, he played with me.
Only on.
He had his own orchestra. He had an orchestra downtown. Wooden Joe, we call it. He was so strong, you know, in the car, and they named him Wooden Joe.
I mean, they wrote a song about that, Wooden Joe. I don't know that. Yeah, I mean, they named Wooden Joe. Well, what band did you play with before you started the Eureka?
Oh, I played in the Hobgoblins.
And about how long had you played in the Hobgoblins before the Eureka?
Oh, I quit the Hobgoblins and made the Eureka. I organized the Eureka band.
But had the Hobgoblins been playing a long time?

The Hobgoblins played a good while. They had a band. And when I joined the Hobgoblins, it was a secret lodge, you know. And when I joined them, a fellow by his name, you ought to know him, George Hampton.
I heard of him.
Well, he's a great musician. He's got a barbershop now right there on, right around the corner there.
How old is he?
Oh, he's about my age or younger.
That's on Claiborne, right?
Yeah, Claiborne.

Claiborne, yes, St. Cook. Uh-huh. Well, we'll find him on the—just as you turn, Claiborne on the riverside of the bank, on this side of the bank. How old does he look to you, my Kenry? I haven't seen him in the—
But he got his barbershop.
That's where Jim Crow gets his hair cut.
Yeah. He's a barbershop. He's a barbershop.
He's a barbershop. He's a barbershop. He's a barbershop.
He's a barbershop.
He's a barbershop.

Oh.
And the silk cap. Yeah, they had the silk gown and the silk gown. Were they blue or green or yellow or what? They were blue. Blue, huh? Yes, indeed.

At night.

At night.

Well then, the Hobgoblins never played funerals.

For funerals.
Did you ever play funerals? Oh, yeah, I did.
Sure. I used to love to play a funeral. Even before the Eureka? Even before the Eureka. I was in the terminal brass band. What was that?
Terminal.
Terminal.
Oh.
Like terminal station. Yeah. I was in that band. I was in that band. In that band.
Well, had you played funerals in the country before you came to the city?
No, ma'am. No, ma'am. They didn't. They didn't use no funerals in the country at that time.
But they were already playing them in the city when you got here?
When I got here, yeah, I knew it.
Did they play most of the funerals or did they play most of the funerals? Did they play more funerals than they do now?
Oh, yeah. Everybody died. And if it belonged to a big society, it had two beds.
Did you ever belong to any of the societies? Yes, ma'am. Which one were you a member of?
Ma'am, I remember the Hobble Cobblets. I remember the Tulane. I was born.
Did you all ever play for women when they died?
No, no, no.
That's what I hear, the things. No, indeed.
That would be a great thing, a woman have a grand, grand funeral.
I wonder what would happen. I never did that.
No, indeed. Well, why not? I never see it. Why not? I don't know, I never see it.
The women used to belong to the society too. Society too, yeah.
You see?
Might be a real humbug at one of those. I've seen lots of things. I've seen a girl got killed and she wanted to be buried in an Indian suit and that sort of thing.
Oh, yeah, I remember. Got killed on Claymore and…
No, I believe that from the town of BC. Buried with her Indian crown. Indian crown, yeah. And he's made up just like an Indian.
Well, the fellow that killed her, he's out. Yeah, he been out. He's been out a good while. He belongs to Muddy's church.
Yeah, he's been out. He belongs to your mother's church you said? No, we call her Muddy. Oh, Muddy. Her church is downtown.
She's a member of, how you call that church? Muddy's church. I know I was down there on St. Anthony Street.
Did you ever play any music in church? Oh man.
I used to go all over playing music in church. Playing church hymns though, you know. Would you play with the brass band or with the orchestra?
Oh yeah, the brass band.

The brass band. The brass band. The brass band. When the saints go marching in, he wrote my guard to thee. What a friend we have in Jesus. We played all that, you know. In church. Didn't play no ragtime. Them was good days man. Them was good days.

Like that.

On line tracks like on railroad.
Oh it's different huh?
Yeah tracks are all buried you don't see no tires. Railroad tires are setting up.
Well the street cars here that might not be as good as the singing and everything.
No it wouldn't be because the tires are buried under the ground. It's leveled. The rail, they have to change the rail but they have to dig all that up and then they bury the tire back down.
What did you do on the railroad?

Well I was labor at first car to clean, coach and fire. Finally World War II came up and the man came down. They took the man I was working for and took him away and put him in service and then sent another man from North Carolina and he wanted to go on a fishing trip. So he found out I could cook. He found out I could cook but I went on a fishing trip. He had never eaten ten line fish before and I ten line fish. I fried fish and we went hard while over there. I made some donuts for him. He had never knew it. It could be you made, you know, cake donuts. I didn't make those other glazed. I made the cake donuts just like you would cake. Made those and he liked it down. I made some French toast for him. The next morning, he had never worked for a living. I said, well the old folks call it lost bread at home. I said, if you go in a restaurant, you would order French toast. From then on, well they and I was cooking on the dirt. He was getting ready to drive the dirt. And I used to go out with him. I'd make my own groceries. Spend seven, eight hundred dollars in one trip. They wanted everything you didn't get at home, you know, because the company was paying for it. And so we had a wreck up here around there. At the Naval Hospital, way up in front of town of the river. And his wife came out there and he told me a picture or something. Geez, so I went on. I had made ice cream. I picked half chicken and I enjoyed it. I picked a little butter, golden brown. My parents said, yeah, never, that chicken tasted good. So after the day, he said, Mac, let me go out again. He said, I want to get a whole case of chicken and I want every man to have half the chicken. So I picked the chicken for him. He ate chicken and a half, a whole, and it was big size. He sprang it. And he ate one and a half. Biscuits, French fried potatoes, ice cream. And I always had the cake or pie or something. I didn't make the cake because they were always moving in the United States. And you make the cake and if you didn't get any vibration at all, they can't fly. They fall. You can't make it flat. So I went for him. There they are. About 14 years.
You say you heard him sing though when?
I heard a couple of numbers, but I don't know if I can remember though. I heard a couple of numbers.
You heard that too, Mr. Parker? You heard people working on the railroad? Me? And singing?
No. My father was working on the railroad. He was a brakesman.
I thought they were 56. I mean they can fly. Yeah. They can.
But you didn't hear them tampin' ties or line and track? Oh yeah, yeah. Yeah, yeah, yeah.
What would they sing? I'd sing anything. Tampin' ties.
I thought maybe you remembered some of the songs. I forgot them. Did they sing anything that got played by bands later? Yeah, they did.
They'd sing. What did friends with bands do? Yeah, they did. And the bands would play that same tune, I see.
Yeah, sure.
They were around the old nine on the old Dale's.
Did they used to sing about the same hymns that they sing now in the churches?
No.
The hymns about the same now in the churches? Yes, ma'am.
Same thing.
I was waiting for them to sing a play the other day, God be with you until we meet again, and they don't play it. No, they didn't. No, they didn't. No, they didn't. No, they didn't.
No, they didn't. Did you all used to play the same kind of music at funerals that they play nowadays?
Yes, they play it.
What?

Music is, we used to get our music from one line, you know? And music is simple. One, two, three, five lines and four spaces. See, that's music. A fella come to you right now and say, you miss this thing? I say, what is music? Well, some fellas can't tell him, cause they wasn't taught to. The music, five lines and four spaces. Yeah, he know you know something.
What were the names of some of the different songs and hymns that the brass bands used to play in the old days?
Oh, different. I mean, we played a lot of different things. I just remember the names of them.
Did you always play ratty music coming back?
Yes, that is our favorite. That's where the second line comes in. That's where the second line comes in.
Well, what is the second line, Mr. Popper?

The fellas behind you are following the band. That's the second line for them. Yeah, you were the larger society in the second line on the band. Sometimes they'd be in front of the members. That's why they don't allow them to have no bands now, behind the funeral. So many fellas then got killed right around the corner, cut up.

And the last band there, the fellas died on the corner. They had a band and they had breakups right there. They was going down to St. Claude Street. And the cut up fell up too bad there. And so they know them. They take it three blocks and then they dismiss them. You know, but you can't carry them directly to the grave. While they bury them, the band be playing. Then on the way back, but them was old days. They were down. Too ratty. They cut up one another.
I don't want to break Jim Horner that day. Is that right? Yeah, right there in the block. Howard?
Howard? Howard?
You know Howard, don't you? Mm-hmm. You know Kid Howard.
Sure.
Cousin of mine.
They wanted to take Kid Howard's trumpet? Yeah, they did, man. How long ago was that about?
About a year, about a year, year, year and a half. About a year and a half.

So that's right up to now. It was summer before last. Mm-hmm. It was summer before last. It was a hot day, I remember. Joe Robichaud was there in the second line. I left early. I was lucky. Well, was there much difference in the second line in different parts of town? It was all the same.
Good evening.
Second line is the same all over town, huh? Same thing. It would be the same across the river and... Everywhere, everywhere.

Everywhere there's a band. Anywhere there's a band, you gonna hear a second line? Anywhere there's a band, they'd make up a bunch of second lines. All them little fellas there, be in front of the band. They leave for me and go across the river. Over the river's the same. Leave me and go uptown, the same thing.

Right after you pass Carrollton, going to Jefferson.

Yeah, I mean, what part of the city is it?
Yeah, I mean, what part of town would you call Carrollton?

Well, that's run into St. Charles and Carrollton and all that. Years ago, that's where all the high rich people lived down that way. But now they mostly live on Lake Vesta. Move out of Lake Vesta or the lakefront now. They move down now. They're mostly going to sell out and rent out now. But all the aristocrats were from St. Charles into Carrollton. All the two out. All right. All right. Now there, there's a very few. Yesterday we saw.
You know where Zion City is?
Zion City?
Mm-hmm.
Zion, Zion, Zion. Well, all that combined into one. You leave one out of Zion City. It's right off from there. That's near the river. It's near the river. It's near the river?
Yeah. It's up near Carrollton? Carrollton. Yeah, that's going around Figue, somewhere around Figue or Apple.
Oh, yeah. There's so many of those sections up there. There's two sections. They combine right in close to one another. Yeah.
Most of the colored people in there. Is that near Cherokee?
Is that near Cherokee? Is that where? No, I'm Cherokee. You get around Figue and Apple Street all up in there.
You see, that runs right into Carrollton Avenue where you go up from there in the back section,
and that's where the colored people are. What churches did you play funerals for? Did you play for Churches for?
Did you play for Churches for? Did you play for Catholic funerals?
No ma'am.
You never played for Catholic?
Catholic don't use no music at all.
Did they use music in the old days?
Not that I know of. But now they don't use no music, not no Catholic.
Well, so you played for Baptist. Did you play for any other religions?
Baptist and sinners, you know.
Sinners?
Yeah, like a club.
Don't belong to church.
Never been baptized.
Didn't play for any Methodist? Didn't play for any Methodist? Yeah. Played for Methodist.
Yeah, all that was the same.
What about Presbyterians? Do they ever have bands? Huh? Do the Presbyterians ever have bands?
Why sure, man. There's very few colored Presbyterians.
There's a few. There was a church back a long time ago.
Now, congregations, I believe. I don't know if they're white congregations.
They have white and colored here in town, I understand. I know one of the colored preachers.
Mm-hmm. I know they had one on Bienville Street, between Gallows, I think. One Bienville between Nero and Tonti.

They used to have a big congregational church called the Central Congregational Church. Do you remember anything about that, Mr. Parker? Uh-huh. The Central Congregational Church, that was one of the big churches. Big colored churches, back in the last century.
No, I don't.
What about the sanctified churches? Did you all ever play funerals for them?
Any of them? Yeah. That's the sanctified right there.
Yes, but did you ever play funerals for them?
The sanctified, yes. Well, play the funerals for them dying in this yard or caught the street. He was sanctified.
And they buried him with music, huh?
Mm-hmm.

Years ago, that's all every male, every student that had was banned. If they didn't have the loan around the vicinity, they passed the sickle box around and collect enough money to buy, to hire the band they had in order for the second line. And they buried him. Oh, they'd pick up enough money. Pick up enough money to hire the band.
Hire a band. That's without a club at all, huh?
Without a club, no. He had to be, you know, well-known. Well-known, that's all.
So-and-so, they had to eat, don't belong to nothing, give me a cigar box. This fella get one, that fella get one. Go around all the ballrooms, everywhere.
Pick up enough money. Sometimes they have two bands, those are what they pick up.
Mm-hmm.
We saw that in Wagaman with the cigar box. Joe Avery's son was out there with the cigar box.
Yeah.
You remember Joe Avery, the tri-ball player?
Yeah, sure.
Yeah, we made his son out there. Uh-huh. Well, were the bands the same size they are now? Same number of men?
Sometimes. Sometimes. Sometimes they'd go out with ten men. Sometimes nine men, you know? Fellas have a job and couldn't get off. Get out there with the nine men. See?
What's the smallest number you could play a parade or a funeral with?
Huh?
What's the smallest number of men you could play a parade or a funeral with?
What were you, twelve?
Twelve would be the smallest.
Twelve men.
What's the smallest brass band you've ever seen?
Huh?
What's the smallest?
Small? Oh, I played in the smallest, seven, eight pieces.
Seven, eight pieces sometimes, huh?
But all substantial men, you know?
Yeah.
Trombone, alto, clarinet, three trumpets.
I saw a parade Sunday with no snare drum. No snare? The Gibson band. And Dave Bailey was playing bass drum. So between the numbers, he'd keep the beat going.
Uh-huh.
On the bass drum. Yeah. That's all. I never saw that before. Who's playing bass drum? Dave Bailey. Yeah? You know, Doc Ernest's brother. Yeah.
Hmm. No snare.

We were talking about churches a minute ago. I understand that the Catholic churches, both the colored and the white people went to the same ones then. Is that true? Do you remember? Well, he wasn't a Catholic. No. That wasn't your church, so you might not remember.
They do it now.
Yeah.

Mm-hmm. They go to the Catholic Church. Now, they have different parishes, you know, but you can visit the church. But I mean, like communion, you have to go to your parish in order to take communion. Well, do you remember back when you first came to the church? Well, you can visit any Catholic Church. You can go to the Baptist or the Baptist or the Petriarch. And even though, as long as you've been in church, you can just imagine you don't have to go personally. But the Catholic has a certain parish, you know. They have a certain parish. And after you go there, well, you can't take communion away else unless you go to the parish.
Well, do you remember back when you first came to the city, whether more of the members of the organizations and stuff wore more in the way of armbands and sashes and cybers?

Yeah, well, on the desk, anyway, like a man's wife would die and he had a piece of crepe he'd wear around the band of his hat. Now, sometimes they had a piece of crepe they'd wear around on the arm of his sleeve for so many months, six months or maybe nine months, then he'd take it off. As long as he, every time you see him dressed up, you had that crepe. That's the memories of his living. That's his wife. And sometimes they'd wear it on the band of the hat. Now, they, they, they, they, they, they, they, they, they, they, they, they, they, they said, then since they're, oh, a woman would use her husband's diet, well, she'd wear black, all black for so many months or so on. But nowadays, they don't do that. They wear that black all the time, maybe six months, a year.
And then they'd get out there and get in the second morning.
Second morning. That's anything with black and white, black and white, second morning, check, black and white. I never heard of that. That's second morning, they call it.
That'd be after the first morning?
After the first morning. First morning is black and then the second morning is check. How long would that last?
Six months.
Last about six months. Second morning.
So that would be about a year and all that would have been. All that. How long have they done that, I wonder?

Ooh, that's only one day. My grandmother, she was sold twice during her slave. She was sold twice during her slave. And my grandfather, that's how he met my grandmother. It was the same man that bought my grandmother, bought my grandfather. And after they got freed, well, they married. I believe they had 14 children. And all of them is gone now but two. That's my mother and brother. No, three. Mother, brother, and sister.
But they were the same kind of morning place? Same kind.
Does your mother live here in the city?
Right there. Look at her in the door. She was in the door just now. That across the street? Right there where you see that mailbox.
Well, she's got a good age on her. No, she don't look old.
Well, what year were you born in?
1908. Well, your mother might remember some good things. We could talk to her sometime. We'd like to. Well, she's home every day.
She's home every day. She's home. No, no. Not home. On Sunday she goes to church and she has to have a cab to take her to church and camp and bring her back.
What is her name again? Ophelia Baptiste.
She's married since the birth.
And she lives at?
1317. That's right there. That's pretty cool up the street.
See, 1317 St. Philip. Yeah, well, we'll get back to see her sometime maybe.
Yeah, she's been home.
Well, did they still have Second Morning when you were in the city or had that...

Well, they had it up until I said they had it up until 1928 after they began to break down. And now there's still some old remembrance. Some of you see it where it's black and then you see Second Morning.
Well, when did they start having the bands less for funerals? I mean, I know, you know, at one point they were having funerals every day and then now they have them very seldom.

Well, that started around, during the depression time, around 32 I think they started breaking off. Because, you know, they didn't have that many musicians and then they couldn't afford the money. Of course, the thing was tight and they were working 12 hours a week on WPA and they couldn't afford the money. So that's going to put down to where it is properly now. But after the war came out, well then that stirred up a little more money. And then they were getting back and back. But during the depression around 32, 34, 33, all that and they couldn't afford the money because the money wasn't in circulation. And they had commodity cards, you had to go there and get your meat and potatoes and apples and so on that way. And you had to go every week and get those things. Well, the money wasn't in circulation. That's when Roosevelt put that out. That's when they had to break the band up.
Well, would you say there are more bands today than there were then?
There were more bands then than there are today.
No, I mean after the depression got started.
There were more bands then than there are now.
Well, did many of them pass out of existence during the depression? Yes, sir.
Yeah, a lot of them. A lot of them quit, had to go to work, they couldn't wait on the music because they couldn't afford the money. Nobody ever hired them. And that made a lot of them give up music.
Mr. Parker, do you remember what bands disappeared during the 30's, brass bands? Do I remember? Which ones went out of existence during depression times?
Oh, no. A lot of the fellas quit playing. There was no money but they made up right away.
What about the Onward band? You know when that stopped?
Oh, yeah indeed. Manny Perez.
Well, when did that stop?

Oh, that broke up long. Buddy Johnson played trombone in that band. Yeah, that was a good band, boy. Manuel Perez. Let me see who played. Who played with Manuel? Bunk. A little buddy called Bunk. What did he play?
Trumpet. I know who he is. Dark fellow.
He's dead now. He played with Manuel and the brass band. Did weddings used to be big affairs?
Do you remember anything about weddings? Did they have bands at weddings in those times? Oh, yeah, man.

You'd be in your bed at 12 o'clock tonight. First thing a band at your door, knocking on your door, waking you up. A band, a string band, call that surprising you. Yeah, get up there. You got, now you, them town, the grocery stay open all night, all open. You had to get up and get drinks for them.
When people got married, did they have music? Yes, indeed. They had the bands there? They had the band. Do people usually get married in the churches or do they get married at their homes?
Oh, the majority of them used to get married at Baptist churches.
Baptist churches.
All you can do, the Catholics don't have no music. Mm-mm.
But the Baptist churches did have the brass bands playing.
Yeah, Baptist believe in music. But then Catholic people.
Well, would you have a brass band or a string band at a wedding? A church.
At the wedding? Oh, at a wedding?
Brass band.
It depends. You know? Orchestra or a brass band. Well did the brass band come into church or did they follow people on the street or what? Well sure they go in church. But they play church hymns.
At weddings?

At weddings. Then they bring the, the one I do, the one got married, and they're not going to do it. The one got married, didn't bring her to our house. But that's a big layout there. But the band was more for that layout than for that thing out.
Well what was laid out there?
Oh, to eat, eat and drink, chicken, biscuits, everything.
Did the band play then or did they just eat after the ceremony was over? They didn't play.
They'd play there too.
They'd eat. And after get through eating they'd have a time.

Be there until the daylight. They had a lot to drink too? Yes ma'am. What tunes would they play at the bride's house? It just depends what church you belong to. No, but at the bride's house. What, what, what tune? Well they had the layout.
At the house. Yeah. What would the band play? What would they play? What song? Oh anything them time. Blues or? Blues, yeah.

Blues or? Well one time a friend of mine came down here on his honeymoon and I got, I got, I got, George Lewis's band to play for him. They played, I ain't gonna give nobody none of my jelly rolls. Yeah.
And then the Eureka Balls had to play for their dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear What was it playing? What songs?
Or anything them time. Blues? Blues, yeah.

One time a friend of mine came down here on his honeymoon, and I got George Lewis's band to play for him. They played I Ain't Gonna Give Nobody None of My Jelly Rolls. And then the Eureka Band played at the airport for this guy going on his honeymoon the other night. And they played I'm Confessing That I Love You.
I broke George Lewis in.
You broke him in, huh?
Yeah, that's an old one I'm confessing I love you. Jelly Rolls, that's an old one. If I had a talking picture, I know another one.
How old is your mother now?
I just remember now, she's about getting close to her 80s.
She's in her 80s?
Yeah, she's in the same place.
And she likes to talk?
Yeah.
Mind is clear and everything?
Yeah.
Good. Where was she from?
A little place they call Moorville. M-O-R-E-A-V-I-L-L-E. Moorville, Louisiana. That's about, I'd say, estimated about 60 or 70 miles this side of Alexandria, Louisiana. I know at Moorville.
Yeah.
It's in between Moorville and Bunky. Oh, yeah.
What was her name when she first came to New Orleans? Uh, Ophelia Pierre.

How do you spell that? O-F-E-L-I-A-P-E-R-R-E, Pierre. She was in the door just now. what do you call that? She used to keep out of it and she'd look at me. I don't go no further than here since I'm not working.
Sometimes you want me to go to the grocery or something, I'll go wash her clothes and then, what do you call that, Willow Bush, they call it wash clothes.

I take a bill around there and wash them and dry and dry and dry and dry and dry. And then you can't do that. What do you call that? What do you call that? Willow Bush, they call it wash clothes. I take a bill around there and wash them and dry and dry and dry and dry. All you have to do is pull them. That's all I have now. If I lose that, I'm finished. Oh, how good. All I can do is, a little bit I can, since I'm not working, she get a little old age. Thank you. But she's gone.
Did she come to the city when she was young?
No, she came when she moved. I don't know if she was young. She lived in Alexandria a long time. Well that's right, you said you were about 20 when you came. Eleven when I came.
Eleven, yeah. In 1920, that's about to think so.
So that she might not remember too much about what the city was like too far away.
Oh, I remember a pretty good bit. They'd take like cotton's jewelry store. That used to be a barber shop on that corner.
Right on the canal.

And you take where the lowest state, that used to be a barber shop on that corner. Right on the canal. And you take where the lowest state, that used to be a barber shop on that corner. Right on the canal. That used to be a bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo bamboo So she might not remember too much about what the city was like too far away?

Oh, I remember pretty good. I shined shoes, I was all in the house. So you take where Cotton's jewelry store, that used to be a barber shop on that corner. Right on the canal. And you take where the Lois State, that used to be a shooting gallery. And where the Sanger is now, that was something like a mummy. You used to go in there and look at all kinds of rubber and wax mummies. And where the F.W. Woolwork, that was a candy store. And coming down toward the Iberville, that was a hardware store. And in between where the parking lot is, right from the lady's club, that was a Tom Anderson's.
What happened to Tom Anderson's?

Tom Anderson's, yeah, he went out of there. The boardroom, huh? Yeah, Tom Anderson's, remember that Boleg used to throw a tray? Yeah, yeah. He kept three trays. Uh-huh. One on top of his head and one in each hand. It was delivered to the Spurgeon, remember, in the, in the, around there where the, that project is? That's where the, in the district, huh?
Yeah.

And he, you know, all the stuff he called out of him, and Boleg used to take three trays. He put one on his head and one in each hand. He kept, and he'd leave them to the door. The first one he'd leave them with it on his hand, see, and then he'd take the other one. He'd still carry that, and when he'd come back and pick up the dishes, he'd put them all on one tray and have them all on one in the head, you know. Never seen the last two times.
Mr. Parker, did you ever play in the district?
Yeah, yes sir.
You played music there? Yeah, I played music in the district. With who? Uh, yeah.
With who, man?
With the, uh, uh, Limon Dauphin. Limon.
Uh, you know him? I know who he is. You told me about him once before. Oh yeah. Where did you play? What place? Where from? Yeah, in the city.
No, you're talking about what the name of the place in the district. Oh, in 25.
You played in 25's, you did? Uh huh. What instrument? I played clarinet. Who else was in the band? In the band at that time?
Uh huh.
Uh huh.
Limon Dauphin, Wooden Joe. Uh, my trammone player, what's his name? Uh, Buddy for two. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.

segments.title: Recording opening at 1314 St. Philip Street
segments.summary: Interviewer states the date, March 29, 1960, and place as recording starts.

segments.title: Military drill groups, brooms and gold-headed canes
segments.summary: Interviewer asks about rifle companies, broom and dumbbell brigades and gold-headed canes; Parker remembers none.

segments.title: Labor Day parades and Parker's sister's schooling
segments.summary: Not enough bands for Labor Day, so country bands filled out the parade; Parker never schooled in New Orleans, his sister did.

segments.title: Jobs for brass bands and the Pickwick band uniforms
segments.summary: Brass bands played ball parks and charity hospital; bands hired extra men in different uniforms.

segments.title: Oriental, Onward and other old bands
segments.summary: Interviewer asks about Oriental, Occidental, Onward and Excelsior bands; Pete Bocage and George Moret mentioned.

segments.title: Wooden Joe in the Eureka band
segments.summary: Parker says trumpeter Wooden Joe played with him in Eureka and led his own downtown orchestra.

segments.title: Hobgoblins and George Hampton
segments.summary: Parker left the Hobgoblins, a lodge band, to organize the Eureka; George Hampton is a barber now.

segments.title: Hobgoblin silk gowns and night parades
segments.summary: Hobgoblins wore blue silk gowns and caps, paraded at night and never played funerals.

segments.title: Playing funerals; the Terminal band
segments.summary: Parker loved funerals, played in the Terminal brass band; no funerals in the country; big societies had two bands.

segments.title: Societies, women's funerals and an Indian-suit burial
segments.summary: Societies, no band funerals for women, and a woman buried in an Indian suit; Muddy's church downtown.

segments.title: Playing hymns in church with the brass band
segments.summary: Parker played hymns like Saints Go Marching In in church, no ragtime.

segments.title: Dance halls, old Jim and Joe Petit
segments.summary: Dance halls, the elder musician Jim whom Parker broke in, Joe Petit, the Tuxedo and Security bands, and Freetown.

segments.title: America's Hall, Geddes Hall and Planters Hotel
segments.summary: Parker does not know the halls named.

segments.title: Cornerstone laying and parades most Sundays
segments.summary: Band leader blew bugle calls at cornerstone laying; social clubs paraded every Sunday; Lent.

segments.title: Lincoln Park and Buddy Bolden
segments.summary: Parker recalls Buddy Bolden playing loud at Lincoln Park and the dancing there; mentions balloon ascents.

segments.title: Balloon ascents and Buddy Bolden
segments.summary: Parker recalls the balloon man in the park, finally named as Buddy Bolden; Sunshine Money was a preacher.

segments.title: Baseball parks and Satchel Paige
segments.summary: Lincoln and Johnson Park were baseball parks with good teams; Satchel Paige's name origin.

segments.title: Churches in Parker's home town
segments.summary: Parker never played for Christians; wakes; he was raised in St. Joseph, a Baptist church, near St. Sophie.

segments.title: Instruments in church and Sydney Brown's sanctified church
segments.summary: Early churches only sang; the sanctified church next door has drums, guitar, tambourine; Sydney Brown plays bass there.

segments.title: Baptisms and church bands
segments.summary: River baptisms at home and street tank baptisms at Easter; the church band kept Parker awake.

segments.chapter: Mac, railroads and the second line
segments.title: Mac's railroad work as a cook
segments.summary: Mac, Parker's neighbour, explains railroad tracks and tells how he became a railroad cook in World War II.

segments.chapter: Mac, railroads and the second line
segments.title: Railroad work songs and hymns
segments.summary: Parker's father was a brakeman; interviewer asks about songs tamping ties and hymns.

segments.chapter: Mac, railroads and the second line
segments.title: Funeral music and the second line
segments.summary: Parker explains reading music, ragtime coming back from funerals and the second line; trouble at funerals.

segments.chapter: Mac, railroads and the second line
segments.title: A recent fight at a second line
segments.summary: Kid Howard's trumpet nearly taken at a recent funeral; second lines are the same all over town.

segments.chapter: Mac, railroads and the second line
segments.title: Uptown sections: Gert Town, Carrollton, Zion City
segments.summary: Mac and Parker describe Gert Town, Carrollton and Zion City.

segments.chapter: Church funerals, band size and mourning
segments.title: Funerals for different churches
segments.summary: Parker played Baptist, Methodist and sanctified funerals, not Catholic, which use no music.

segments.chapter: Church funerals, band size and mourning
segments.title: Cigar-box collections to hire a funeral band
segments.summary: Mac and Parker explain bands hired by passing the cigar box for a well-known man.

segments.chapter: Church funerals, band size and mourning
segments.title: Size of brass bands
segments.summary: Parker says bands went out with nine or ten men; he played in seven or eight-piece bands.

segments.chapter: Church funerals, band size and mourning
segments.title: Catholic parishes and mourning customs
segments.summary: Mac explains Catholic parishes and crepe, black and second mourning.

segments.title: Mac's grandparents and mother Ophelia Baptiste
segments.summary: Mac tells of his enslaved grandparents, his birth in 1908 and his mother Ophelia Baptiste across the street.

segments.title: Depression decline of brass bands; Onward band
segments.summary: Mac says funerals with bands fell off around 1932; Parker recalls Manuel Perez's Onward band with Bunk.

segments.title: Weddings and bands
segments.summary: Parker describes serenades, church weddings, feasts and music, and George Lewis.

segments.title: Mac's mother's origins and his chores
segments.summary: Mac says his mother was born Ophelia Pierre in Moreauville and describes his own chores.

segments.title: Downtown Canal Street memories and Tom Anderson's
segments.summary: Mac remembers Canal Street shops, shining shoes, Tom Anderson's and the waiter Boleg.

segments.title: Parker playing in the district
segments.summary: Parker says he played clarinet in the district at 25's with Limon Dauphin and Wooden Joe.
